identity.resolved_name: Seraphim of Sarov (born Prokhor Isidorovich Moshnin)

saint.name: St. Seraphim of Sarov
saint.summary: In September 1804 three peasants beat a hermit nearly to death in the forest near Sarov, looking for his money. He had put down his axe rather than fight them. They found an icon and some potatoes, and he begged that they go unpunished. Seraphim of Sarov spent thirty years in the forest, on a stone, in silence, and behind a locked door with an oak coffin in the entry. Then he spent his last years greeting every stranger, in any season, with "My joy, Christ is risen!" What was the treasure the robbers never found, and how did a man who once hid his face from passers-by end his life with a crowd at his door?
saint.biography:
On 12 September 1804, in the forest a few miles from the monastery of Sarov, a monk named Seraphim was working near his hut when three peasants came up to him and demanded money. He was not a weak man. He had an axe in his hands, and he was strong enough to use it. For a moment the choice was his. Then, the story goes, he remembered the words of Christ, that all who take the sword shall perish by the sword. He put the axe down on the ground, crossed his arms, and said, “Do what you need to do.”

One of them snatched up the axe and struck him on the head with the butt of it, and he fell. They dragged him toward his hut, beating him as they went, tied his hands and feet, and left him in the entry. Then they went inside and tore the place apart looking for money. They found an icon and some potatoes, and they ran.

The next morning, while the brothers of Sarov were at the Liturgy, Seraphim came back to the monastery. He had spent the night in his cell, and now he made his way in with great difficulty, covered in blood, with several teeth knocked out. He stayed there about five months, and he walked bent over for the rest of his life. When the three men were found, he went to the abbot and begged him not to punish them. If they were punished, he said, he would rather leave the monastery himself.

The robbers had been sure there was treasure somewhere in that hut. Twenty-seven years later, on a winter day in the same forest, the old monk they had crippled crouched in the snow beside a landowner. There he explained, in the language of a merchant, exactly what his treasure was and how a person acquires it. By then he had spent more than thirty years in the forest and behind a locked door, and for part of that time he had refused to speak a word to anyone. Yet in his last years people came to his door day after day, and he met them, rich or poor, at any season of the year, with the same words: “My joy! Christ is risen!”

In 1903 the Russian Orthodox Church declared Seraphim of Sarov a saint, and the tsar himself helped carry his coffin. How did a hermit who once fell on his face in the forest rather than meet a passer-by end his life with a crowd at his door? And what had he found out there, alone, that the robbers could not? The answer begins in a merchant’s house in Kursk, where a boy learned early which goods pay best.

A Merchant’s Son in Kursk

He was born Prokhor Moshnin, the youngest of three children of Isidor and Agafia Moshnin, a merchant family of Kursk. The year is not certain. The old Lives give 19 July 1759, and his gravestone counted his age to match. But parish records published in 1903 list him as a boy of fourteen in 1768, and the Church now dates his birth to 1754. His sister Paraskeva and his brother Alexei were older. Isidor took on building work, and he had undertaken a stone church in Kursk dedicated to St. Sergius, built, one Life says, to a plan by the architect Rastrelli. He died when Prokhor was still very small, and the church stood unfinished. Agafia took the work on herself and finished it.

Two moments from his childhood were remembered ever after. When he was about seven, he fell from high up on the unfinished church to the ground below. His mother ran down, sure that she would find him dead. Instead she found him standing on his feet, without a scratch.

A few years later, at about ten, he fell seriously ill, and the illness went on and on. The Life written in 1863 says that in a dream the Mother of God promised to come and heal him. Soon afterward the people of Kursk carried their wonderworking icon of the Mother of God of the Sign through the town in procession. That day a heavy rain fell, and the procession, probably to shorten its way and keep out of the mud, turned aside and passed through the Moshnin yard. Agafia carried her sick son out, and he was held up under the icon as it went by. From that day he began to recover.

He grew up in the family trade. His brother Alexei kept a shop, and Prokhor worked in it, selling leather straps, tar, rope, bast shoes, and ironware. The shop stayed with him. More than half a century later, explaining to a visitor how a Christian should spend his life, he would reach for the shop: “I come from a family of Kursk merchants,” he said. “When I was not yet in the monastery, we used to trade in the goods that brought us the most profit.”

On feast days he gathered the other young men of the town and read spiritual books aloud to them. He made friends with a fool for Christ who lived in Kursk, one of the wandering ascetics who hide their prayer behind an appearance of madness. Diveyevo, the community he would one day care for, kept a tradition about a Kursk fool for Christ of that time. When Prokhor was three, it says, the man met Agafia with the child and told her that her boy would be “a strong intercessor before the Holy Trinity.” Before long Prokhor and several young merchants of Kursk were talking of leaving the world together and becoming monks.

A Copper Cross for the Road

To leave, a merchant’s son needed a release from the town society of Kursk, and Prokhor obtained one. Then came the farewell with his mother. They sat down together, and he bowed down to her feet. She gave him a copper cross. He wore it openly on his chest for the rest of his life.

He went first to Kiev, to pray at the relics of the saints in the Caves Monastery. There a recluse named Dositheus gave him his blessing and sent him on to Sarov, a monastery in the forests. He arrived on 20 November 1778, the eve of the feast of the Entry of the Mother of God into the Temple. The abbot, Father Pachomius, received him, and he was put in the care of the treasurer, Father Joseph, as a novice.

Sarov gave him the ordinary work of a young monk, and he took it up. He rang the bells and baked the prosphora, the bread for the Liturgy. As a carpenter he carved crosses out of cypress wood, and with his own hands he made an altar of cypress for the monastery’s hospital church. Then, in 1780, his body began to swell with dropsy, and the illness kept him in his cell for about three years. It grew so serious that Pachomius offered to bring a doctor and have him bled. Prokhor refused.

“I have given myself over to the True Physician of souls and bodies, our Lord Jesus Christ, and to His Most Pure Mother, the Most Blessed Virgin Mary.”

— Prokhor to Abbot Pachomius, 1780, in the Life by Hieromonk Sergius (1841)

So Father Joseph served an all-night vigil and the Liturgy for the sick novice, and then he brought him Holy Communion in his cell. The oldest Life, written by a monk who knew Seraphim for fifteen years, says only what happened next: the following night came “a divine visit.”

The Night of the Divine Visit

Later Lives fill in what the first one left plain. The Mother of God appeared to him, they say, in a light beyond telling, with the apostles Peter and John. She laid her hand on his head and touched his thigh with her staff. The water that had swollen his body drained away, and he recovered. Decades afterward, by the account the Diveyevo sisters kept, he told a woman named Ksenia, who served in the church, about that night. Then he made her put her hand into a hollow that had been left in his thigh.

The novice who had refused the doctor was tonsured a monk on 13 August 1786 by Father Pachomius, with Father Isaiah standing as his sponsor and spiritual father. He received the name Seraphim. Before long the bishop of Vladimir ordained him a deacon, and for the next several years he served at the altar almost every day. He often spent whole days in church. During the services, the Lives say, he sometimes saw what others did not, and one Holy Thursday, serving at the Liturgy, he saw Christ Himself surrounded by the heavenly hosts. He described that vision himself, and one of the early Lives kept his account. He also began to slip away at night to a cell in the forest, about three miles from the monastery, to pray alone.

On 2 September 1793 he was ordained a priest. His legs were swollen, and in the autumn of 1794 he asked Pachomius for permission to leave the monastery and live alone in the forest. A manuscript copy of one early Life, kept at the Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra, tells a strange story about that departure. The abbot, it says, sent a retired soldier to wait on the road and strike the young monk as he passed. Seraphim fell, got up, and turned the other cheek, and the man did not strike him again.

Whatever happened on the road, Seraphim reached the forest. He would stay there, with only short breaks, for some sixteen years.

Lions and Leopards in the Forest

His hut stood in the forest, about three miles from the monastery. He dug garden beds, cut his own wood, and read: the Gospel and the Epistles, the Ladder of St. John Climacus, St. Basil, St. Ephraim the Syrian, and the Philokalia. For food he grew potatoes and vegetables. In time he gave up even the monastery’s bread, and for more than two years, he told someone shortly before his death, he lived on snyt, a wild herb that he dried for the winter. On the eve of every Sunday and feast day he came to the monastery, and at vespers he went back to the forest with a week’s bread. In the first week of Lent he stayed at the monastery and ate nothing at all until Saturday.

He knew what he was choosing. Monks who live in a community, he used to say, fight the enemy as if with doves, but in the desert they fight as if with lions and leopards. The one who lives in the desert must be as if crucified on a cross. He knew, too, that the hermit’s life had its critics. “They forbid us the desert,” he said once, “but our first father, John the Forerunner, was a desert-dweller.”

The world did not forget him out there. Around 1796 he was offered the post of archimandrite, the head of a monastery, at Alatyr. He begged Father Isaiah to refuse it for him, and another monk of Sarov, Abraham, went in his place. The forest had its own trials. The oldest Life says that the devil, in the night, lifted him into the air and threw him down on the floor. Once a tree fell on him and bent his back.

Then he did something that no one at Sarov knew about while it was happening. He took two stones, one in his hut and one out in the forest. By day he stood on the first, and by night on the second, with his hands raised to heaven. Over and over he repeated the prayer of the publican in the Gospel: “God, be merciful to me a sinner.” He kept it up for a thousand days and a thousand nights. A later abbot of Sarov, writing in 1848, said that he stood without moving for seventeen hours a day. His hair matted like felt, and his legs were damaged for the rest of his life. Answering a letter from a bishop of Tambov years later, the abbot Nifont noted in his draft reply that no one had known of the thousand days on the stone.

A brother who heard about it said that such a thing was beyond human strength. Seraphim pointed him to St. Symeon the Stylite, who had lived on top of a pillar, and spoke of the help that comes from above.

“That ascetic stood on a pillar for forty-seven years, and are my labors anything like his? … When there is tenderness of heart, then God is with us.”

— Seraphim to a brother of Sarov, in the Life by Hieromonk Sergius (1841)

That was the man the three peasants found at his work in September 1804: a monk with a garden, an icon, and some potatoes, and nothing else worth stealing.

Bent for the Rest of His Life

For about five months after the beating, Seraphim stayed in the monastery. His head and his chest had been broken. The Lives say that the Mother of God came to him again in that illness, with the apostles Peter and John, as she had come to the sick novice twenty-four years before. One later account even gives the words she spoke about him: “This is one of my kind.” Seraphim himself said less. He told one brother only that he had been healed by the intercession of the Mother of God.

The three men turned out to be serfs of a landowner named Tatishchev, from the village of Kremenki. Seraphim begged the abbot to let them go unpunished, and he meant it: he would sooner be sent away from Sarov himself. They were not punished. Some time later a fire burned down their houses, and they came to Seraphim in tears to ask his forgiveness.

He never stood straight again. For the rest of his life he walked bent over, leaning on an axe, a hoe, or a stick. In later years the people who came to see him were received by a stooped old man. When he could walk again, he went back to the forest.

In 1807 Father Isaiah died. He had stood beside Seraphim at his tonsure and guided him for more than twenty years, and with his death Seraphim did something new. He stopped speaking. For about three years he did not say a word to anyone. If someone came to his hut, he did not come out. If he met someone on a forest path, he fell face down on the ground and stayed there until they had gone by.

Once a week, on Sunday, a brother from the monastery brought him food, most of all in winter, when his garden gave nothing. The two of them never spoke. Seraphim let him know what to bring next time by what he laid on the tray: a piece of bread, or a little cabbage. There was no word and no blessing, only the tray.

In May 1810 the silence in the forest came to an end. Seraphim came back to live in the monastery, under Abbot Nifont. He went into his cell, and the next day he shut the door.

An Oak Coffin in the Entry

For the next five years almost no one saw him. He kept no fire in his cell. He wore chains. His hair grew so matted that when it was finally cut, it came off whole, like a cap. A brother left his food in the entry, and in that entry stood an oak coffin, which Seraphim kept there for himself. He prayed beside it, and the oldest Life says that he sat in his cell as if he were already in the grave.

His days had a strict shape. On Mondays he read the Gospel of St. Matthew, on Tuesdays St. Mark, on Wednesdays St. Luke, and on Thursdays St. John. He made a thousand prostrations a day and prayed the Jesus Prayer. He knew the lives of the saints in the Menaion so well that he could later retell whole stretches of them from memory.

In September 1815 he opened his door to his first visitor from outside, the former governor of Tambov. Little by little, over the years that followed, the door stayed open longer, though he himself did not leave the cell until 1825.

The people who came found a man they did not expect. He bowed to the ground before every visitor, poor or rich, and kissed the hands of lay people. He kissed his guests and greeted them, whatever the month, with the Easter greeting, “Christ is risen!” Each of them was “my joy.” He gave them dried crusts of bread, water he had blessed, and oil from his lamp, and the people who knew him said they never saw him sad or downcast. Asked for permission to take his portrait, he refused: “Who am I, poor Seraphim, that I could allow a portrait to be taken of me?” Even so, a portrait of him was painted in 1828, by a painter named Serebryakov.

Not everyone at Sarov was glad of him. For some of the brothers, the oldest Life admits, he was hard even to look at. Someone told him to his face that people took scandal from him, and he answered with a play on words: “I am not scandalized that some profit from me and others are scandalized.” When he had to correct someone, the oldest Life says, he did it meekly, without harsh reproaches. His severity he kept for himself. “We must always, in every case, try to cut off the causes of vanity at the very start,” he said. When he was praised, he answered with the psalm, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to Your name give glory.” When people thanked him for a healing, he turned it away. “Is it Seraphim’s business,” he asked, “to put to death and to make alive, to bring down to hell and to bring up again?”

One of the first healings that his Lives record took place in 1823. Mikhail Manturov had lost the use of his legs, and he came to Seraphim for help. Seraphim answered him with a condition.

“My joy! If you believe so, then believe this too: that to one who believes, everything is possible from God. And so believe that the Lord will heal you as well, and I, poor Seraphim, will pray.”

— Seraphim to Mikhail Manturov, in the Life by Archimandrite Seraphim (Chichagov), 1903

He anointed Manturov’s legs with oil, and Manturov was healed. Then Seraphim asked something of him in return, and it was not small: “Now, my joy, give to the Lord everything you have, and take on yourself a poverty of your own choosing!” In the years ahead Manturov’s money would build a mill and a church for a community of women whom Seraphim had not yet been given. That gift was coming, and it would bring him out of his cell for good.

Sent Out by the Mother of God

Seraphim did not leave the enclosure on his own judgment. He asked God to confirm it first. On 25 November 1825, the feast of St. Clement, the Mother of God appeared to him, the Life of 1903 says, with St. Clement and St. Peter of Alexandria, and released him from his enclosure. Motovilov wrote down Seraphim’s own telling of that day. Walking through the forest along the little river Sarovka, Seraphim saw her there, and she gave into his care the women of Diveyevo. In that account she showed him how their community was to be built, down to a ditch around it and the names of eight sisters.

He built himself a new hut on the bank of the Sarovka, a little more than a mile from the monastery, and from then on he spent his days there. People who saw him going back and forth remembered the figure: a bent old man in a white linen smock, with an axe in his hand, and on his back a sack. The sack held stones and sand, and with them he carried the Gospel. When someone asked him why he carried the stones, he answered with a line from St. Ephraim the Syrian: “I torment him who torments me.” He used to sing an antiphon of the Church about the unceasing longing for God that comes to those who live in the desert.

The visitors came nearly every day now. One of the Diveyevo sisters remembered finding him with flies on his face and blood on his cheeks.

“Don’t touch them, my joy. Let every breath praise the Lord!”

— Seraphim to a Diveyevo sister, in the Life by Archimandrite Seraphim (Chichagov), 1903

Stories about what he knew began to travel around Sarov. One, which the monks passed on only as something they had heard, concerned a peasant whose horse had been stolen. The man ran to Seraphim. The old monk took the peasant’s head and pressed it to his own, then told him which village to go to and which gate to look behind, and warned him to guard himself with silence. His own brothers got plainer answers. One of them once asked him why the monks of their day did not live as strictly as the ancient ascetics. “Because we have no resolve,” Seraphim told him. “If we had the resolve, we would live as the fathers who shone in ancient times.”

For ordinary people he asked much less, and he made it simple. On rising from sleep, he told them, every Christian should stand before the icons and say the Lord’s Prayer three times, “Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos” three times, and the Creed once. Before going to bed, they should do the same. Through the day, at work or on the road, they should keep repeating the Jesus Prayer. “Walking and sitting, working, and standing in church before the service begins, coming in and going out,” he said, “keep this unceasingly on your lips and in your heart.” It was a rule a peasant could keep in a field. And it promised the very thing he had gone into the forest to find. “By calling on the name of God in this way,” he said, “you will find peace, you will reach purity of spirit and body, and the Holy Spirit will dwell in you.”

The hermit who had once lain face down on a forest path rather than meet a passer-by now spent his days among people. He had not given up the desert. He carried it on his back, in a sack of stones. But the Mother of God had given him a family to look after, and it was waiting for him at Diveyevo.

The Orphans of Diveyevo

Diveyevo was a community of women not far from Sarov. Mother Alexandra Melgunova had founded it, and Seraphim named her as its founder. He called its sisters his orphans. On 9 December 1825, the feast of the Conception, he prayed with a group of them at his old hut in the forest, and from that day the community of the mill began.

It began with a mill. Over the next year and a half Seraphim had the posts and timber cut and carried with the horses of Sarov, and the sisters carried timber with their own hands. On 7 July 1827 the mill ground its first grain. He sent six sisters to live beside it, named Paraskeva Stepanovna as their senior, and gave them Father Vasily Sadovsky as their confessor. Then he set the sisters to dig a ditch around the place of the vision. They dug it for three years and planted gooseberries on its earth bank, and they called it the Ditch of the Mother of God.

He ran his little community with common sense and a dry humor. He kept the widows and the young unmarried sisters apart. “In a community,” he said, “it is easier to manage seven maidens than one widow.” When one of the sisters, Paraskeva, wanted to leave, he answered her with his own life.

“I, matushka, have gone through the whole of monastic life, and never once, even in thought, have I left the monastery.”

— Seraphim to Sister Paraskeva of Diveyevo, in the Life by N. V. Elagin (1863)

The sisters remembered his healings as part of daily life. Evdokia Nazarova had been paralyzed for two years when he told her to go out and rake hay, and she was healed. Another sister, Paraskeva Semyonovna, was coughing when he threw water from his sleeve over her. “Why are you coughing?” he asked. “Stop, enough!” “I can’t, Batiushka!” she said, and the cough stopped. Near Sarov, at the spring called the Theologian’s Spring, he saw in a vision the Mother of God strike the ground with her staff, and water flowed. He dug out a well there, and he told a man named Anastasius that she had promised to bless its water more than the waters of Bethesda in Jerusalem.

His care for these women cost him. The sisters knew that some of the monks of Sarov disliked the whole Diveyevo work. “They drove him and persecuted him constantly because of us,” Sister Evdokia remembered. “And he, our dear one, bore it all good-naturedly, even laughed, and often, knowing all about it, joked with us.”

In 1831, the year of the cholera, Seraphim treated a peasant who was sick with it. He used what he had: the icon of the Mother of God called Tenderness, which hung in his cell, blessed water, and a piece of prosphora. The man recovered. Merchants from Kursk came too, and the old man who had once sold rope and tar in his brother’s shop raised his hands and told them, “There is nothing better than the monastic life.”

On the feast of the Annunciation in 1831, one synaxarion says, the Mother of God came to him for the last time. It was the twelfth time in his life, and she came with St. John the Baptist, St. John the Theologian, and twelve virgin saints.

He had chosen his family long ago. In 1831, pointing to the icons of Christ and the Mother of God in his cell, he said, “These are my kin; to my living kin I am already a living corpse.” Yet he still asked a visitor that winter to pray for his parents, Isidor and Agafia. The visitor was Anthony Medvedev, abbot of the Vysokogorsk monastery, who had come in terror of death. Divine Providence, Seraphim told him, was entrusting him with a vast lavra. “Do not forsake my orphans,” he added. One of Anthony’s monks wept when Seraphim told him, “You will soon part from your hegumen.” Anthony became abbot of the Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra, and years later he helped bring the first Life of Seraphim into print.

That September, a landowner was carried into the forest to see the old man, so weak that he could not stand.

A Landowner Under a Pine

His name was Nikolai Motovilov, and for more than three years he had been nearly paralyzed. In the first days of September 1831 he was brought to Sarov, and on the 9th he was set down under a pine tree by the Sarovka. Motovilov wrote down afterward what Seraphim said to him, and it began with a disclaimer.

“But I’m not a doctor, you know,” Seraphim told him. Then he asked Motovilov whether he believed, and when he had his answer, he said, “Ah, if you believe, then you are already well!”

Motovilov was healed. In the years ahead he would become a benefactor of Diveyevo and one of the people who did most to keep Seraphim’s memory. Since the age of twelve he had carried one question with him: what is the aim of the Christian life? Seraphim, it turned out, already knew that.

Brighter Than the Noon Sun

Motovilov wrote down this conversation too, and his account, which was not published until seventy years later, is the only record of it. It took place on a Thursday in November 1831. The day was grey, and the snow was falling. In a clearing in the forest, Motovilov sat on the stump of a tree that had just been cut down, and Seraphim crouched in front of him, facing him. The Lord had shown him, the old man said, what Motovilov had wanted to know since he was a boy. Then he told him.

“The true aim of our Christian life,” he said, “consists in acquiring the Holy Spirit of God.” Prayer, fasting, vigils, and every other Christian work are good in themselves, he explained, yet doing them is only the means; the aim is the Spirit. And to explain what he meant by “acquiring,” the son of the Kursk merchants went back to the shop.

“Acquiring is the same as obtaining. … The aim of the worldly life of ordinary people is the acquiring, or making, of money. … The acquiring of the Spirit of God is also capital, only a capital of grace, and eternal.”

— Seraphim to N. A. Motovilov, November 1831, in Motovilov’s account (published 1903)

A trader, he said, deals in the goods that pay best, and a Christian should do the same with the virtues. Other good works may be beyond a person’s strength or means, but one of them is within reach of anyone. For prayer, he said, “everyone always has the means: rich and poor, noble and simple, strong and weak, healthy and sick, righteous and sinner.” And when the Spirit comes in answer to prayer, a person should stop asking Him to come. Seraphim made the point with a joke about a guest. If you invited him to visit, he said, and he came, and you went on inviting him all the same, he would have to wonder, “What is the matter with him? Has he gone out of his mind?”

Then Seraphim took Motovilov firmly by the shoulders.

“We are both in the Spirit of God now, batiushka, you and I. Why aren’t you looking at me?”

“I can’t look, batiushka, because lightning is pouring from your eyes. Your face has become brighter than the sun, and my eyes ache with the pain.”

— Seraphim and N. A. Motovilov, November 1831, in Motovilov’s account

He tried to describe it for readers who had not been there. “Imagine,” he wrote, “in the middle of the sun, in the most dazzling brightness of its noonday rays, the face of the man who is talking with you.” The light spread out for several fathoms around them and lit up the snow. Seraphim had not even made the sign of the cross, he told Motovilov. He had only said in his heart, “Lord, make him worthy to see clearly, with bodily eyes, that descent of Your Spirit.”

Then the old man began to ask him questions. What did he feel? “I feel such stillness and peace in my soul,” Motovilov said, “that no words can express it!” What else? “An uncommon sweetness!” What else? “An uncommon joy!” And what else? “An uncommon warmth!” Here Seraphim stopped him. “But we’re sitting in the forest,” he said. “It’s winter outside, there’s snow under our feet, and more than an inch of snow on us.” Motovilov insisted: it was warm, he said, like a bathhouse when water is thrown on the stove. And then there was the smell.

“When my mother was still alive, I loved to dance and go to balls … my mother used to sprinkle me with perfume that she bought in the best shops of Kazan, but even that perfume does not give off such fragrance.”

— N. A. Motovilov to Seraphim, November 1831, in Motovilov’s account

Seraphim smiled warmly. “I know it myself, batiushka, just as well as you do,” he said, “but I ask you on purpose.” What Motovilov had seen, the old man told him, was given to him to understand “not for yourself alone, but through you for the whole world.” “We have become very inattentive to the work of our salvation,” Seraphim said. Yet people have seen God and the grace of His Spirit in waking truth, and not in a dream or a fantasy. The Lord seeks a heart filled with love for God and for neighbor, and that is the throne on which He loves to sit.

The robbers of 1804 had torn his hut apart looking for treasure and found potatoes. Here in the snow was the capital he had been gathering all those years, on the stone, behind the locked door, in the long silence, and he had just shown it to someone else. He had a little more than a year left.

Crowns Are Being Prepared

He knew it. In the spring of 1832 an officer named Ladyzhensky came to see him with his sisters, on his way to China. His wrist hurt him, and when Seraphim gripped it, the pain went away. Then, three times over, Seraphim told him, “We will not see each other again.” That same year he told a boy from Vladimir that he would enter a monastery and be freed from serfdom, and in time the boy became a monk named Vasily. A bishop, Arseny of Tambov, visited him in his last year and was even let into his private place of prayer, a closet so small that it held one person standing.

He lit many candles before the icons in his cell. Asked why he burned so many, he answered with the prayer he said as he lit them. “Lord, remember all those people, Your servants,” it went, “for whose souls I, poor one, have lit these candles and lamps to You.” Near the end of 1832 he told a brother to blow out one of the candles. When it went out, he said, “Just so, they will not see me either.”

At Christmas, a week before he died, a visitor named Bogdanov found him standing by his oak coffin, leaning on it, holding a lit wax candle, and extremely cheerful. He greeted his guest as “your God-loving one.” He had already gone out and measured the place for his grave, beside the altar of the Dormition cathedral. To Brother Pavel, the monk in the next cell, he said something stranger. “While I live there will be no fire,” he told him. “But when I die, my death will be revealed by a fire.” Of Pavel himself he said that he would enter the Kingdom of God without difficulty, for the simplicity of his heart: “He never judges anyone and envies no one.”

On 1 January 1833 he went to the Liturgy in the hospital church, the church of Sts. Zosima and Savvaty, for which he had once built an altar of cypress with his own hands, and he received Communion. Then he went round the church and lit a candle before every icon. He kissed each of the brothers and blessed them, and he left them with these words:

“Save yourselves, do not lose heart, stay awake: this day crowns are being prepared for us.”

— Seraphim to the brothers of Sarov, 1 January 1833, in the Life by N. V. Elagin (1863)

He went out by the north door. That day he sent two hundred rubles to Diveyevo, to Sister Paraskeva Ivanovna, for bread, because the sisters had run out. In the evening Brother Pavel heard him singing in his cell. He was singing the hymns of Easter.

At about six the next morning, 2 January, Pavel smelled smoke at Seraphim’s door. It was hooked shut from inside, and a novice named Anikita broke the hook. Inside, in the dark, linen and books lying on the bench were smouldering. In the church, where the brothers were already at the Liturgy, a boy came and whispered the news. They found Seraphim on his knees before his icon of the Mother of God, the one called Tenderness, in his white robe. His arms were crossed on his chest and his head was bowed. A copper cross hung at his neck, the kind his mother had blessed him with in Kursk. His eyes were closed, and his face, the brothers said, looked alive with prayer. The book before him was partly scorched. His body was still warm.

He was seventy-eight years old, by the parish records of Kursk; his gravestone would say seventy-three. A story spread later that at the Glinsk hermitage, Father Filaret saw a light rising in the sky that night and said, “That is the soul of Father Seraphim ascending!” Nearer home, there was a smaller sign. A priest named Theoktist, whom Seraphim had sent on his way the day before, set off in his sleigh, and its fastening broke, so he stopped at Diveyevo. There the sisters asked him to serve the memorial service, just as Seraphim had told him: “So you will serve in Diveyevo.”

Eight Days in the Cathedral

For eight days his body lay open in the Dormition cathedral at Sarov. Thousands came, people of every rank from the neighboring provinces, and the crowd around the coffin was so thick that the candles beside it went out from the heat. Then Abbot Nifont buried him beside the grave of Mark the recluse, and an enamel icon of St. Sergius from the Lavra was laid with him. No speeches were made.

The people who had known him set about remembering him. In the autumn of 1834 Motovilov traveled to Kursk to collect what the town still remembered of the Moshnin family. While he was there, he bought two thousand apple trees for the orchard at Diveyevo. Four monks who had lived beside Seraphim wrote Lives of him, each after leaving Sarov. Sergius had known him at Sarov for fifteen years, Ioasaf for twelve, Georgy for five, and Avel for three. The first, by Sergius, was finished in 1837 and ran straight into the censors. Metropolitan Seraphim of St. Petersburg distrusted its miracles and held it up. Metropolitan Philaret of Moscow defended it, and Bishop Arseny of Tambov, who had known Seraphim, reviewed it. Much of the struggle passed through Anthony, now abbot of the Lavra and Philaret’s friend, the same man to whom Seraphim had said, “Do not forsake my orphans.” The Life was printed at last in December 1841, with some passages about his visions and healings softened along the way.

He had refused to let a portrait be taken of him. In October 1843 one of those four monks, Avel, printed a lithograph of him anyway. The Lives also began to collect stories, and not all of them could be checked. A later abbot of Sarov, Isaiah, wrote in 1849 that some of what one of the four, Ioasaf, had published was “not in keeping with the truth known to us.”

Among the stories told of him is one of a bear that he fed at his forest hut. It comes from one witness, a Diveyevo sister named Matrona Pleshcheeva, and a file in the Moscow archives reports that on her deathbed she said Ioasaf had taught her to tell it. This life does not rely on it.

In 1861 a chapel was built over his grave beside the cathedral, and the same year the sisters of Diveyevo, whose two communities had merged in 1842, became a convent. His orphans had not been forsaken. In Sarov and Diveyevo, people went on asking for his prayers, and many of them said that the prayers were answered.

The Tsar Who Carried the Coffin

The first surviving document proposing to declare him a saint was written on 27 January 1883, during the coronation year of Alexander III. It went from G. K. Vinogradov to Pobedonostsev, who seems to have received the idea coolly. Even so, from February 1892 to August 1894 a Church commission gathered accounts of healings and help through Seraphim’s prayers from twenty-nine dioceses. It investigated ninety-four cases, and most of them were confirmed by the sworn statements of witnesses. Hundreds more letters lay unrecorded in the Sarov archive.

The push that finished the matter came from the throne. On 19 July 1902 Nicholas II made known his wish to see the cause brought to an end. Sergei Witte later wrote that the tsar demanded it of Pobedonostsev personally, probably at the empress’s urging. Pobedonostsev blamed Archimandrite Seraphim Chichagov for putting the idea into the tsar’s head, and General Kireev recorded him calling Chichagov “a great schemer and rogue.” Chichagov was the man who had gathered the memories of the Diveyevo sisters into a chronicle and a Life. He later became a metropolitan, was shot in 1937, and is himself now venerated as a saint.

On 11 January 1903 a commission of bishops, among them Metropolitan Vladimir of Moscow, opened Seraphim’s coffin. What they found was a skeleton. The body had decayed, and Metropolitan Anthony of St. Petersburg had to publish a statement that a saint’s body need not be incorrupt. On 26 January the tsar wrote by hand on the report that he had read it with true joy and deep compunction. Three days later, on 29 January, the Holy Synod declared Seraphim a saint.

That summer Sarov filled with people. The estimates of the crowd for the July celebrations run from a hundred thousand to three hundred thousand. From 25 June a hieroschemamonk named Simeon kept a journal of the healings reported there. On 3 July the relics were carried from the grave to the hospital church of Sts. Zosima and Savvaty, the church where Seraphim had served his last Liturgy. On 16 July a deaf-mute girl named Polya spoke, and the crowd gave her coins. A blind child was given the water to drink and cried out, “Mama, mama, I can see you!”

The journal and the reports of those weeks read like a list from the Gospels. A man who had walked on crutches for more than twenty years burned them at the spring. A widowed Cossack named Anna Ilyeva, blind for nineteen years, said that she could see. A bedridden young woman felt her strength return after the third time she was dipped in the water. Peter Bondarenko, a veteran of the Turkish war from Warsaw, was nearly blind. He wiped his eyes with a handkerchief that had lain on the relics, and his sight came back. An old man who had been carried in by two others stood up straight.

On 18 July Metropolitan Anthony served the last memorial service for Seraphim as a departed monk; from then on the Church prayed to him as a saint. The next morning was 19 July, the day the old Lives gave as his birthday. The relics were laid in a cypress coffin given by the tsar and the empress and carried in procession, and Nicholas II was one of the men who carried it. That week two churches were consecrated in his honor, one at his old forest cell and one, on 22 July, at Diveyevo. That same summer the empress bathed in the spring, praying for a son. Alexei was born the next summer. Two officials, Mosolov and Witte, later tied his birth to Sarov, though who first urged the empress to go to Sarov is disputed. That year, too, Motovilov’s account of the conversation in the snow was printed for the first time. Sergei Nilus, who published it, said he had found it in a box of papers given to him by Motovilov’s widow.

Some of what was told about that summer belongs to tradition. One story says that Seraphim had left a sealed letter “for the fourth sovereign who will come to Sarov,” and that it was handed to Nicholas II in 1903; no one knows what it said. Another says that Seraphim had given Motovilov a sealed packet with the message that Motovilov’s wife would live to see the whole imperial family come to Diveyevo.

Twice Seraphim had been laid to rest with prayer and ceremony, once by his own brothers and once by an emperor. The third time, the people who came for him did not come to pray.

Mittens in a Museum Storeroom

In November 1920 the Soviet of the Temnikov district voted to open the shrine. On 17 December 1920 the officials did it and wrote a report. They listed a figure of cotton wadding dressed in brocade and silk, slippers set with amethysts, and old, dark-brown bones, with a vertebra, a rib, and parts of the lower jaw missing. The red hair of his head and beard had been tied to the skull with ribbons. In 1922 the remains were taken to Moscow and given to the Museum of Religious Art at the Donskoi Monastery. After that, they dropped out of sight.

The places he had loved went the same way. Diveyevo was closed in 1927, and the monastery at Sarov was shut at about the same time. In 1946 Sarov itself disappeared from the maps, turned into a closed city for building nuclear weapons. In the 1950s the Dormition cathedral, beside which he had measured out his grave, was blown up.

Even the spring near Sarov was not left alone. In the 1950s, by the account of the faithful, it was filled with cement. A story told about the 1960s says that soldiers in the closed zone saw an old man in a white cassock near the spot. The story goes on that a bulldozer driver at work there saw an old man come out of the forest. “Basil, why are you destroying my spring?” the old man asked, and then, “You will not succeed.” And the spring came back.

Seventy years after the shrine was opened, in the autumn of 1990, a set of unknown remains turned up in Leningrad. They lay in the storerooms of the Museum of the History of Religion, which was housed in the Kazan Cathedral. The remains had no inventory number. On 5 December 1990 a commission of two bishops, Eugene of Tambov and Arseny, examined them. The chief evidence was a pair of mittens, embroidered with the words “Venerable Father Seraphim” and “Pray to God for us.”

On 11 January 1991 the relics were handed back to the Church, and Patriarch Alexy II served the Liturgy over them in the Kazan Cathedral. In February they went by train to Moscow, where thousands followed them in procession to the Epiphany Cathedral, and some of the nuns of Diveyevo were there to see it. On 28 July a procession set out from Moscow, and on 1 August 1991 Seraphim came home to Diveyevo. There Mother Margarita, ninety-two years old, lit the candle that, by the nuns’ tradition, Seraphim himself had once given them. The Patriarch placed the icon of the Mother of God from Seraphim’s cell in a church at his own residence in Moscow.

My Joy, Christ Is Risen

His relics rest at Diveyevo now. The Russian Orthodox Church keeps his feast twice a year: on 2 January, the day of his death, and on 19 July, the day his relics were uncovered in 1903. The Russian Church still keeps the old Julian calendar, so in the civil calendar those days fall on 15 January and 1 August. At the spring of St. Seraphim, pilgrims still plunge three times into the water, even when the air is below freezing, and many of them tell of healings.

In July 2003, for the hundredth anniversary of his canonization, his relics were carried in procession from Diveyevo to Sarov. A cross was raised on the site of the destroyed Dormition cathedral, beside which he had once been buried.

Sarov has remained a closed city, home to Russia’s Federal Nuclear Center. In 2006 the Synod decided to reopen the monastery there, and in September 2007 a prayer service was held for the first time to Seraphim as the patron of nuclear scientists. The iconographer Pavel Busalayev has put the strangeness of it plainly. In Sarov, he said, people “simultaneously pray for peace throughout the world and make things that can blow that very same world to pieces.”

The three robbers of 1804 were sure that the hermit had a treasure, and they were right. They looked for it in a hut with an icon and some potatoes, and he had it with him all along. He spent thirty years gathering it on a stone, in silence, and behind a door with a coffin in the entry. Then he spent his last years giving it away to anyone who came. One saying remembered in his name comes from later collections of memories, and it puts the whole of those last years into one sentence. “My joy, I beg you,” he told a monk, “acquire a peaceful spirit, and then thousands of souls around you will be saved.”

The people still come, to Diveyevo and to the spring. They come to an old man who walked bent over and bowed to the ground before every one of them. He met them all, in every season of the year, with the same words: “My joy! Christ is risen!”

A Note on the Sources

The year of Seraphim’s birth is disputed. The Lives of 1841 and 1903 give 19 July 1759, and his gravestone gave his age at death as 73 years, 5 months, and 12 days, which fits that year. Kursk confession records published in 1903 list him as fourteen in 1768, and the Russian Church now uses 1754; one early Life gives 19 June as the day. The conversation with Motovilov on acquiring the Holy Spirit survives only in Motovilov’s account. Sergei Nilus published it in 1903 from papers given to him by Motovilov’s widow. Nilus cut some pages when he reprinted it in 1905, and in the same year he also published the Protocols of Zion. The Russian scholar A. Strizhev traces the text to Motovilov’s own notes and calls Motovilov a man “not without oddities,” and the prophecies about Russia that later circulated from the same papers are doubtful and are not used here. The story of the bear is told in the Lives of Ioasaf (1849) and Elagin (1863) on the word of one witness, Matrona Pleshcheeva. A file in Metropolitan Philaret’s papers is reported to say that on her deathbed she told the head of her community and her confessor that Ioasaf had taught her to tell it. We have not seen the file ourselves, only the articles that cite it. The 1841 Life says only that the boy fell “from the height of the building,” and the Russian Wikipedia article says that the bell tower named in later versions did not yet exist. Sources disagree on the date of the thousand days on the stone, and some place it in 1807–1810. The 1841 Life dates the tonsure to 13 August 1786, and the Synod act of 1903 gives 18 August. The same Life dates his return to the monastery to 9 May 1809, while the Sarov archive gives 8 May 1810, which this account follows. In the Life of 1903 the vision of 25 November 1825 is a dream-vision that released him from his enclosure, while Motovilov’s note places it by the Sarovka. A saying about a peaceful spirit appears in later collections of memories, and not in the four early Lives. Some English accounts say that his relics vanished miraculously in 1926; this account follows the Russian records of the 1920 opening and the 1990 discovery. The volume of Spiritual Instructions printed under his name in 1863 is mostly drawn from the Church Fathers and is not quoted here as his own words.

How This Life Was Researched

This life draws on twenty-one sources in Russian and English. They include the first printed Life of 1841, written by a monk who lived fifteen years at Sarov, and the Life of 1863, built from the monastery archive and dozens of named witnesses. The Life of 1903 was compiled from the memories of the Diveyevo sisters and Motovilov’s notes. Other sources include Motovilov’s own account, the Holy Synod’s act of 1903, a journal of the healings recorded at Sarov that summer, and a dated chronicle of his life. The researchers flagged fifteen details as missing from the usual English accounts. Except for a few short passages quoted from modern English sources, the translations from Russian are our own.

This list gathers the accounts of healings, visions, and foreknowledge attributed to Seraphim of Sarov, with their sources and their status. Each entry says who reported the event and how the report was treated. It makes no claim of scientific proof, and it does not dismiss any account. Only the cases examined by the Church commission of 1892–1894 were investigated and accepted by the Holy Synod, and our sources do not name them one by one. Every other entry is a report, and its status line says who made it. Where the sources disagree, the entry says so.

Cases examined by the Church

The Church’s inquiry before the canonization of 1903 examined healings attributed to Seraphim’s prayers after his death. Our sources give its numbers and its verdict, not the individual cases.

Ninety-four cases before the Synod, 1892–1894

From 3 February 1892 to August 1894 a Church commission gathered reports of healings and help through Seraphim’s prayers from twenty-nine dioceses. It investigated ninety-four cases, and most of them were confirmed by the sworn statements of witnesses. Its report went to the Holy Synod through the bishop of Tambov in 1895, and two more collections followed in 1897. Hundreds of other letters lay unrecorded in the Sarov archive. In its act of 29 January 1903 the Synod wrote that the cases left no doubt about their validity.

Status: investigated by a Church commission and accepted by the Holy Synod for the canonization of 1903.

Source: Holy Synod, Act of 29 January 1903 (English translation, ROCOR), https://synod.com/english/pages/heritage/canonofsersar.html

During Seraphim’s life

These accounts come from the Lives written by monks who knew him, from the memories of the Diveyevo sisters, and from Motovilov’s papers. They include healings, visions, and words of foreknowledge.

A fall from the unfinished church, Kursk

When Prokhor was about seven, he fell from high on the church his family was building in Kursk. His mother ran down, sure that she would find him dead, and found him standing, unhurt. The Life of 1841 says only that he fell “from the height of the building.” The bell tower named in Elagin’s Life of 1863 did not yet exist at the time, according to the Russian Wikipedia article, which treats that detail as legend.

Status: recorded in the Lives; the bell-tower detail is a later addition.

At about ten (the Brookline synaxarion says nine), Prokhor fell gravely ill for a long time. Elagin’s Life says that in a dream the Mother of God promised to visit and heal him. Dropsy cured after “a divine visit,” Sarov, 1780

As a novice he swelled with dropsy, an illness that the monk Avel says lasted about three years. Near the end of 1832 Seraphim had a brother blow out a candle and said, “Just so, they will not see me either.” He measured his grave beside the altar of the Dormition cathedral. teachings.teachings:
Seraphim is not known to have written a book. His teaching survives in the words that people who knew him remembered: the monks of Sarov who wrote the first Lives, the sisters of Diveyevo, and Nikolai Motovilov. A volume of Spiritual Instructions printed under his name in 1863 is mostly a collection of passages from the Church Fathers, so it is not used here. The seven themes below follow his remembered words, with the place and the reason for each. The translations from Russian are our own.

Acquiring the Holy Spirit

The aim of the Christian life, Seraphim taught, is to acquire the Holy Spirit of God. Prayer, fasting, vigils, and good works are good, but they are the means and not the goal. He explained the word “acquire” as a merchant would: worldly people work to make money, and a Christian works to gather a capital of grace that is never lost. Some works are beyond a person’s strength or means, so he urged people to put their effort where it pays best.

“Prayer, fasting, vigil, and every other Christian work, however good they are in themselves, are not the aim of our Christian life merely in the doing of them, though they serve as the necessary means for reaching it.”

— Seraphim to N. A. Motovilov, November 1831, in Motovilov’s account (published 1903)

He said it in a snowy forest clearing near Sarov in November 1831, to Motovilov, who had wanted to know the aim of the Christian life since he was twelve. The conversation survives only in Motovilov’s account, which was published in 1903, and its authenticity is debated. Seraphim’s own life fits it: he spent about thirty years in the forest and in his locked cell in prayer, and then he gave his last years to the people who came to his door.

Prayer anyone can keep

Seraphim held that prayer is open to everyone, “rich and poor, noble and simple, strong and weak, healthy and sick, righteous and sinner.” For lay people he set a short rule. On rising, a Christian should stand before the icons and say the Lord’s Prayer three times, “Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos” three times, and the Creed once, and do the same at night. Through the day he or she should keep repeating the Jesus Prayer.

“Walking and sitting, working, and standing in church before the service begins, coming in and going out, keep this unceasingly on your lips and in your heart.”

— Seraphim on the Jesus Prayer, in the Life by Archimandrite Seraphim (Chichagov), 1903

The rule is recorded in Chichagov’s Life, written from the memories of the Diveyevo sisters and Motovilov’s notes. Its promise, he said, is peace, purity of spirit and body, and the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. His own rule in his enclosure was far heavier: a Gospel a day, a thousand prostrations, and the Jesus Prayer. In the forest he stood on a stone for a thousand days and nights repeating the publican’s prayer, “God, be merciful to me a sinner.”

Joy and the Easter greeting

Seraphim greeted visitors, in every season, with the Easter greeting, “Christ is risen!”, and called them “my joy.” The people who knew him said they never saw him sad or downcast. One saying remembered in his name joins inner peace to love for others.

“My joy, I beg you, acquire a peaceful spirit, and then thousands of souls around you will be saved.”

— Seraphim to a monk, as given in a later collection of memories of him; not found in the first Lives

The saying appears in a later collection of memories, not in the four early Lives, so its exact wording is less certain than the rest. He lived the joy to the end: a week before his death a visitor found him leaning on his coffin with a lit candle, extremely cheerful, and on his last evening a brother heard him singing the hymns of Easter.

Cutting off vanity

Seraphim treated vanity as the fault to catch first. He called himself “poor Seraphim,” turned praise back to God, and refused credit for healings.

“We must always, in every case, try to cut off the causes of vanity at the very start.”

— Seraphim, in the Life by Hieromonk Sergius (1841)

The Life of 1841, by a monk who knew him for fifteen years, records the saying. When praised, he answered with the psalm, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to Your name give glory.” Around 1796 he begged his spiritual father to refuse for him the post of archimandrite at Alatyr, and he refused to let a portrait be taken: “Who am I, poor Seraphim, that I could allow a portrait to be taken of me?”

Forgiving those who harm us

The sources we read record no saying of his on forgiveness. What follows is the example of his life, not his own doctrine. When three men came to rob him in 1804, he was holding an axe and could have fought. Remembering that all who take the sword shall perish by the sword, he put it down.

“Do what you need to do.”

— Seraphim to the three robbers, 12 September 1804, in the Life by N. V. Elagin (1863)

They beat him nearly to death, and he walked bent for the rest of his life. He begged the abbot not to punish them and said he would rather leave the monastery himself, and later the men came to ask his forgiveness. In the same spirit, a Diveyevo sister remembered, he bore the hostility of some Sarov monks “good-naturedly, even laughed.”

Trust in God in sickness

Seraphim taught the sick to put their faith in God first, and he gave his own prayer along with it.

“I have given myself over to the True Physician of souls and bodies, our Lord Jesus Christ, and to His Most Pure Mother, the Most Blessed Virgin Mary.”

— Prokhor to Abbot Pachomius, 1780, in the Life by Hieromonk Sergius (1841)

He said it as a young novice swollen with dropsy, when his abbot offered a doctor and bleeding, and the Lives say he recovered after receiving Communion and a divine visit. Later, the sick who came to him were asked first whether they believed. To Mikhail Manturov he said that “to one who believes, everything is possible from God … and I, poor Seraphim, will pray,” and to Motovilov, “If you believe, then you are already well!”

The desert and resolve

Seraphim loved the hermit’s life and knew its cost. Monks in a community, he said, fight the enemy as if with doves, but in the desert as if with lions and leopards. When a brother asked why the monks of his day lived less strictly than the ancients, his answer was about the will.

“If we had the resolve, we would live as the fathers who shone in ancient times.”

— Seraphim to a brother of Sarov, in the Life by N. V. Elagin (1863)

His first answer to that brother was, “Because we have no resolve.” He lived in the forest from 1794 to 1810, kept three years of silence, and spent fifteen years in his cell, and in his old age he still carried a sack of stones on his back. When a Diveyevo sister wanted to leave her community, he told her that he had never once, even in thought, left the monastery.

did_you_know.fact: Three peasants who beat him nearly to death in 1804 searched his hut for money and found only an icon and some potatoes.
For about three years he spoke to no one, and if he met someone in the forest he lay face down until they had passed.
He kept an oak coffin in the entry of his cell and prayed beside it.
In 1990 his lost relics were identified in a Leningrad museum storeroom by mittens embroidered “Venerable Father Seraphim.”
Sarov became a secret nuclear weapons city in 1946, and in 2007 Seraphim was first prayed to there as patron of nuclear scientists.

gaps: Birth year is disputed (1759 in the Lives of 1841 and 1903 and on the gravestone; 1754 from Kursk confession records published in 1903 and now used by the Church). birth_year is left null under the Directus rule for disputed dates; set 1754 if the owner prefers the Church’s date.

The Conversation with Motovilov (the source of the light-in-the-snow scene and the “acquiring the Holy Spirit” teaching) survives only in Motovilov’s account, published by Nilus in 1903; its authenticity is debated. The biography and teachings attribute it.
The saying “acquire a peaceful spirit, and thousands around you will be saved” was found only in a modern summary of memories (S8 own-words), not in the early Lives.
Chichagov’s Chronicle (Letopis, 1896) was not read directly; its material comes through the azbyka chronicle compilation.
Elagin’s chapters 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 were not read in detail; ch. 11–12 hold posthumous accounts that are missing from the miracles list.
OrthoChristian’s 1903 account was read only to word 3,000 of 5,251; more 1903 healings likely exist.
Individual cases from the 1892–1894 commission are not named in the sources read.
Current relic location after 1991 is taken as Diveyevo; the 2003 procession and any later moves were not checked in detail.
Image: no candidate has a verified rights page; nothing was downloaded.
No troparion, kontakion, or akathist was researched for related.prayers.
The patronage of nuclear scientists rests on the Russian Wikipedia article and a news feature; no Church decree was found.
The Manturov healing is dated 1823 by Russian Wikipedia; the own-words researcher placed it about 1827.
Some 1903 healing entries give little detail beyond the name and illness, because the source does.
